clue.text: Flipping freezing in Kendal, surprisingly like Switzerland?

indicators.note: the reversed piece is set inside the rearranged town name
the letters of the town come out in a surprising, unexpected order
flipping turns the synonym for freezing over, so it reads backwards

parts.note: freezing means cold

explanation.surface: Someone in a chilly Cumbrian town remarks that it feels as icy and enclosed as the Alps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British swearword qualifying 'freezing', but it is the reversal signal; 'in' puts DLOC inside LANKED, made by 'surprisingly'. Kendal is a town in Cumbria, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Switzerland has no coastline at all, being entirely surrounded by other countries; the question mark flags it as an example.

clue.text: Universal anger about politician becoming mediator

indicators.note: the first two pieces go round, encircling, the politician

parts.note: U is the film-rating abbreviation for universal
ire is a literary word for anger
MP, Member of Parliament, is a politician

explanation.surface: A furious public row over an MP ends with someone stepping in to calm things down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts UIRE around MP.
explanation.definitionFit: An umpire is an arbiter called in to settle a dispute between two sides, as a mediator does.

clue.text: Under pressure upset son talks foolishly

indicators.note: in a down answer the remaining pieces sit beneath, under, the letter for pressure

parts.note: P is the physics abbreviation for pressure
to upset someone is to rattle them
S is the genealogical abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A son, rattled under pressure, starts babbling nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under pressure' reads as a stock phrase, but in this down clue it means the rest follows P.
explanation.definitionFit: To prattle is to chatter idly and childishly, so prattles is a synonym for talks foolishly.

clue.text: Wood American enters with Alan quite regularly

indicators.note: the abbreviation for American goes into the rest of the build
regularly takes every other letter of the words Alan and quite

explanation.surface: An American joins a man called Alan, quite regularly, perhaps at a timber yard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the even letters of ALAN QUITE, giving LNUT; W (with) goes in front and 'enters' puts A (American) between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Walnut is a prized hardwood timber used for furniture, so it is a type of wood.

clue.text: Rude Italian gentleman, blowing top over social worker

indicators.note: in a down answer the first piece sits over the second
blowing one's top loses the first letter of the Italian title

parts.note: signor is the Italian title for a gentleman
the ant is a social insect, and a worker ant is the classic example

explanation.surface: An Italian man loses his temper and is rude to a social worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blowing top' drops the S of SIGNOR; 'social worker' is an ant, the social insect, not a welfare officer.
explanation.definitionFit: In informal British use ignorant means discourteous or ill-mannered, a synonym for rude.

clue.text: Follow story on the radio

indicators.note: on the radio the word is heard rather than seen, so we take its sound

parts.note: a tale is a story

explanation.surface: Keep up with a serial being broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: To tail someone is to shadow them secretly, so it is a synonym for follow.

clue.text: Stir cocktail

definitions.meaning: a tequila ... is a cocktail, often just called a ...

explanation.surface: An instruction to mix a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Both stir and slammer are slang for jail, and a slammer is also a fizzy tequila drink banged on the bar.

clue.text: Have influence giving support to national topic

indicators.note: in a down answer the second piece sits under, holding up, the first

parts.note: a national of a country is one of its subjects
to matter is to count, to have influence

explanation.surface: A citizen's backing lends weight to a national issue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'national' is a noun here, a citizen.
explanation.definitionFit: Subject matter is the theme or content dealt with, a synonym for topic.

clue.text: Hound one obtaining bread in Kabul?

parts.note: the Afghan is a breed of hound
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A dog gets hold of a loaf in the Afghan capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bread' is slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: The afghani is the currency of Afghanistan, whose capital is Kabul; bread is slang for cash.

clue.text: Criminal triad I contend is brainwashed

indicators.note: criminal suggests the letters are wrongly, crookedly, arranged

explanation.surface: A gang member insists that a triad has had its mind controlled.
explanation.walkthrough: A triad here is a Chinese crime gang, fitting 'Criminal'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be indoctrinated is to have beliefs drilled in uncritically, the same as being brainwashed.

clue.text: Foul by China in game

parts.note: foul means bad
Minton is a famous make of English porcelain, a china

explanation.surface: A player commits a foul against China during a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' is pottery, not the country; Minton is a Staffordshire porcelain maker.
explanation.definitionFit: Badminton is a racket sport, so it is an example of a game.

clue.text: Worked hard having no time to get drunk

indicators.note: having no means the letter for time is left out

parts.note: toiled means worked hard

explanation.surface: Someone laboured so long they had no time left except to get tipsy.
explanation.definitionFit: Oiled is informal slang for intoxicated, from being well lubricated with alcohol.

clue.text: Call up Derek over purchases being returned

indicators.note: being returned means the hidden letters are read backwards
the words purchases, takes a grip on, the letters we need

explanation.surface: Derek is reminded of past buys as goods come back to the shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'purchases' looks like shopping but means grips; 'being returned' reverses EKOVE, hidden in 'derEK OVEr'.
explanation.definitionFit: To evoke a memory is to summon it to mind, the same as calling it up.

clue.text: Teach girl strangely lacking in energy

indicators.note: strangely means the letters come out in an odd new order

explanation.surface: A tutor finds a pupil oddly listless.
explanation.definitionFit: Lethargic describes someone sluggish and listless, without vigour.

clue.text: Doctor i.e. a GP using animals in tests

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so these letters are altered

explanation.surface: A family doctor experiments on creatures in the lab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like the GP's job title but is a verb, to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Guinea pigs were long used as laboratory subjects, so the phrase means any test subject.

clue.text: Proceeds with article probing ultimately fraudulent Cambridge college

indicators.note: the article pokes into, probes, the other letters
ultimately takes the final letter of fraudulent

parts.note: King's is a college of Cambridge University
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An investigation proceeds into a crooked Cambridge college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Proceeds' looks like a verb but is the noun, money taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Takings are the money received by a business, its proceeds.

clue.text: Monicker of English chap, taken up following prison

indicators.note: the reversed piece comes after, following, the slang word for prison

parts.note: nick is British slang for a prison or police station

indicators.note: in a down answer taken up means read upwards, reversed

parts.note: a chap is a man

explanation.surface: An Englishman released from jail gets a new alias.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken up' reverses E + MAN to NAME.
explanation.definitionFit: A monicker is an informal name or label, as a nickname is.

clue.text: Favourite bank is comparatively small

parts.note: a pet is a favourite, as in teacher's pet
a bank is a row or tier, as of seats

explanation.surface: A preferred lender turns out to be rather minor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bank' is a row, not a lender.
explanation.definitionFit: Pettier is the comparative of petty, meaning trivial or minor, so more small-minded or smaller.

clue.text: Cured pork pate can't spread

indicators.note: spread means the letters are spread about and rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that a meat pâté won't go on the toast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spread' looks like what one does with pâté but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Pancetta is Italian salt-cured pork belly, similar to bacon.

clue.text: Habit of PPS, say, to defend Conservative

indicators.note: to defend is to surround protectively, so the first piece wraps the second

parts.note: a PPS, post-postscript, is an addition to a letter; say marks the example

explanation.surface: A habit of a Parliamentary Private Secretary is backing the Tories.
explanation.walkthrough: PPS looks like a Parliamentary Private Secretary, a British ministerial aide, but here is a post-postscript.
explanation.definitionFit: An addiction is a compulsive dependency, a strong habit.

clue.text: Some Montenegrins identified behind bars

indicators.note: some of the letters, running across the two words, give the answer

parts.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A few Balkan nationals have been identified as being in jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Inside is informal for in prison, which is being behind bars.

clue.text: Concert hall, empty old one in ruins

indicators.note: empty removes the inside of the word old, leaving its outer letters
in ruins means the word one is wrecked and rearranged

explanation.surface: A disused old music venue lies derelict.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Greece an odeon was a roofed building for musical performances.

clue.text: Run rings round Oxford University idiot

parts.note: a twit is an idiot

explanation.surface: A fool at Oxford is easily outclassed.
explanation.definitionFit: To outwit is to outsmart; running rings round someone is an idiom for that.

clue.text: Symbolic inscription on gift for broadcaster Bruce, perhaps

parts.note: a gift tag reads to followed by the recipient
Ken Bruce is a British radio presenter, long on BBC Radio 2; perhaps marks him as one Ken

explanation.surface: A tag reads 'To Ken', on a present for the radio host.
explanation.walkthrough: Ken Bruce is a well-known British radio DJ.
explanation.definitionFit: A token gesture is a nominal or symbolic one, done for show.

clue.text: Disc barely covered by Kansas radio station

indicators.note: the middle piece is wrapped, covered, by the state abbreviation

parts.note: KS is the postal abbreviation for Kansas

indicators.note: barely means stripped bare, its outer letters gone, leaving the middle of disc

explanation.surface: A record barely gets airplay on a Kansas station.
explanation.definitionFit: Kiss is the name of a British commercial radio station, Kiss FM.

clue.text: Best place to make contact with darling Mark

parts.note: sweet can mean darling, lovely
a spot is a mark

explanation.surface: Advice on where to get in touch with a beloved called Mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' poses as a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweet spot on a bat or racket is the point where striking the ball works best.

clue.text: Objection about locking up opponents began again

indicators.note: the turned word locks up, encloses, the opponents
about means the word for objection is turned round

parts.note: a demur is an objection
in bridge East and South are opposing players, E and S

explanation.surface: After objections, a match with rivals detained restarted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' gives RUMED and 'locking up' puts the pair inside it; 'opponents' rests on bridge, where East and South sit on opposing sides.
explanation.definitionFit: To resume is to start again after a pause, so resumed means began again.

clue.text: Understood how judge may appear after lawsuit's conclusion

indicators.note: the description of the judge comes after the final letter
the conclusion of a word is its last letter

parts.note: British judges traditionally wear wigs, so appear wigged

explanation.surface: A courtroom scene once a case has ended.
explanation.walkthrough: British judges wear horsehair wigs in court.
explanation.definitionFit: Twigged is British informal for grasped or realised, so understood.
